annotations.keyFindings: In a rural service, 58 percent of eligible patients received pre-hospital tranexamic acid; single-paramedic attendance and age over 65 were linked to lower administration, and 11 percent of doses were given after three hours.
annotations.limitations: One service; injury time estimated for 18 percent; no hospital outcomes.

annotations.keyFindings: Benefit on death from bleeding falls with every 15 minutes of delay and is not seen after three hours; no overall increase in vascular occlusive events.
annotations.limitations: Mostly in-hospital administration; pre-hospital timing inferred.

annotations.keyFindings: Ambulance-hospital linkage matched 91 percent of directly conveyed trauma patients but 78 percent of transfers; unmatched patients were older and more severely injured.
annotations.limitations: One region; linkage variables may differ here.

annotations.keyFindings: Paramedics withheld tranexamic acid because of uncertain injury time, single-crew workload and concern about older patients taking anticoagulants; they rarely learned patient outcomes.
annotations.limitations: Two services; recall of recent calls.

annotations.keyFindings: Among patients aged 65 or over, 30-day venous thromboembolism was 3.1 percent after pre-hospital tranexamic acid against 2.4 percent without, with a wide interval.
annotations.limitations: Registry of trauma-unit admissions only; confounding by severity.

claims.text: In a rural ambulance service, 58 percent of eligible injured adults received tranexamic acid before hospital arrival.
claims.passage: Fifty-eight percent received tranexamic acid before hospital arrival, at a median of 52 minutes after injury.
claims.interpretation: A planning value for compliance and a sign that a compliance audit may find missed doses.

claims.text: The benefit of tranexamic acid on death from bleeding falls with delay and is not seen after three hours.
claims.passage: the benefit fell by about 10 percent for every 15 minutes of delay, with no benefit seen after three hours
claims.interpretation: Timing is part of the audit standard, not only whether the drug was given.

claims.text: Ambulance to hospital linkage matched 91 percent of directly conveyed trauma patients but only 78 percent of transfers.
claims.passage: Linkage matched 91 percent of trauma patients conveyed directly but only 78 percent of those transferred between hospitals
claims.interpretation: An outcome analysis needs an agreement covering all sites and hand follow-up of unmatched records.

claims.text: In older trauma patients, 30-day venous thromboembolism was 3.1 percent after pre-hospital tranexamic acid and 2.4 percent without.
claims.passage: Venous thromboembolism within 30 days was recorded in 3.1 and 2.4 percent respectively
claims.interpretation: A safety question an outcome analysis would have to address, with confounding by severity.

synthesis: Five retrieved records from the fixture search, appraised at abstract level; a second search channel failed and returned nothing. Paramedics describe uncertain injury times, single-crew workload and concern about anticoagulated older patients as reasons for withholding the drug. In one rural service, a little over half of eligible patients received pre-hospital tranexamic acid and one in nine doses was late. Pooled trial data show the benefit falls with every 15 minutes of delay and is absent after three hours. Linking ambulance to hospital records misses more of the older, more severely injured and transferred patients, and a registry of older patients shows a small, imprecise excess of thromboembolism.
gradeRationale: High certainty about the timing effect from pooled trials, but low certainty for the questions this network would answer: compliance and outcomes in rural pre-hospital care rest on single observational studies with missing data and selection by linkage.
summary: Five retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; overall certainty low for the local questions.
